## The specification menu {#the-specification-menu .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: menu-table
#| output: asis
# The twelve decisions of the menu (data/menu_options.csv), with the options
# that the curve keeps and the others grouped by the judgement of the course.
judgement_txt <- c(other_question = "another question", weaker_answer = "a weaker answer",
                   check = "a check", unavailable = "not in the data")
level_txt <- c(estimand = "1 – Estimands", measurement = "2 – Measurement",
               estimation = "3 – Estimation")
# dplyr::summarise() with .by keeps the order of the menu, where
# datawizard::data_summary() would sort the decisions
off_txt <- menu_opts |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!on_curve) |>
  dplyr::summarise(txt = paste0(paste(label, collapse = " · "), " *(", judgement_txt[dplyr::first(judgement)], ")*"),
                   .by = c(axis, judgement)) |>
  dplyr::summarise(off = paste(txt, collapse = "; "), .by = axis)
menu_rows <- menu_opts |>
  datawizard::data_filter(on_curve) |>
  dplyr::summarise(level = dplyr::first(level), decision = dplyr::first(decision),
                   on = paste(label, collapse = " · "), .by = axis) |>
  dplyr::left_join(off_txt, by = "axis") |>
  dplyr::mutate(off = dplyr::coalesce(off, "–"),
                level = dplyr::if_else(level == dplyr::lag(level, default = ""), "", level_txt[level]),
                line = paste0("| ", level, " | **", decision, "** | ", on, " | ", off, " |"))
cat(c("::: {.fs-50}", # r-style: keep – writes the Markdown of the table
      "| Level | Decision | On the curve | Off the curve |",
      "|:--|:--|:--|:--|",
      menu_rows$line, ":::"), sep = "\n")
```

::: {.small}
Five decisions keep more than one option, and they cross into the **`r nrow(curve)`** specifications of the curve. The [decision map](../cases/trust/map.html) gives the reason for every option.
:::

::: notes
Here is the menu. It is the full list of decisions that any analyst of this claim has to take, twelve of them, at three levels. Level 1 decides which question is asked: the outcome, what is held constant, the weights that decide whose answers count for how much, and the respondents. Level 2 decides how the variables are measured, which covers concern, the rule for unanswered items, education, the votes and the missing answers. Level 3 decides how the answer is reached: the comparison within countries, the standard errors and the scale of the result. Every option on the right was considered and left off the curve for a stated reason, because it answers another question, answers this one less well, is a check, or cannot be built from the data. The decision map on the site gives the reason for each.
:::

## The curve of 192 {#the-curve-of-192 .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **Outcome** – distrust of parliament · of politicians · of the legal system · the mean of the three
- **Adjustment** – no controls · demographics · outlook and ideology · the controls of the paper
- **Weights** – none · design weights · design and population weights
- **Unanswered items** – every item answered · the answered items
- **Countries and rounds** – an intercept for every country-round · one for every country, with a shift for every round
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
4 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 2 = **`r nrow(curve)`**. The reference specification is the one closest to the model of the paper: **`r fmt_num(curve_ref$b, 3)`** points of distrust per point of concern, *t* = `r fmt_num(curve_ref$stat, 2)` on `r curve_ref$df` df with errors clustered by country, n = `r fmt_n(curve_ref$n)`.

```{.r}
try_spec(outcome = "parliament", controls = "paper", weights = "none",
         items = "complete", fe = "country_round")
```
:::

::: notes
Five of the twelve decisions keep more than one option on the curve. The outcome, four ways. The adjustment, four nested sets of controls, from none to the full set of the paper. The weights, three ways. The rule for unanswered items, two. And the comparison within countries, an intercept for every country-round or one for every country with a shift for each round. [advance] Four times four times three times two times two is a hundred and ninety-two specifications, and the course has fitted every one. The reference specification is the one closest to the model of the paper: distrust of parliament, all its controls, no weights, every item answered, an intercept for every country-round. It gives point one seven five, against the point one seven of Table 3. Every argument of try underscore spec defaults to it, so changing one thing means changing one argument.
:::

## Ground rules for the menu {#ground-rules-for-the-menu .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **Change one decision at a time**, and hold the others at the reference specification. When a result moves, you can then say what moved it
- **An option off the curve is refused** by `try_spec()`, with the reason from the menu and the page that teaches it. Asking for one is part of the exercise
- **One sign convention:** every estimate is points of distrust per point of concern, so a value above zero is the direction of the claim
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The estimand statement on the [decision map](../cases/trust/map.html) rewrites itself as you choose. A change in a bold phrase asks another question, a change in a green phrase measures the same question differently, and a change in the second sentence reaches the answer another way.
:::

::: notes
Three ground rules before you touch the menu. First, change one decision at a time and hold the others at the reference. That sounds restrictive, but it is what makes the class chart readable, because when a result sits somewhere surprising we can say what put it there. Second, if you ask for an option that is off the curve, try underscore spec refuses it, tells you why, and names the page that teaches it. Trying one is part of the exercise, because the refusal is where the reasoning lives. Third, one sign convention binds everybody: every estimate is in points of distrust per point of concern, so above zero is the direction of the claim. [advance] And the decision map on the site shows the estimand statement rewriting itself as you choose, which tells you whether a choice changes the question or only the way of answering it.
:::
